currentUse: St. Bernard remains an active Roman Catholic parish at 5734 10-1/2 Mile Road, with regular Sunday and Friday Masses. It is administratively clustered with Saint Ann-Saint Ignatius and St. John Cantius. Current Lithuanian-language worship is not established.
summary: St. Bernard in Irons began as a Roman Catholic mission in 1920 and received its first resident pastor in 1948. Historical descriptions identify strong Lithuanian and Bohemian participation, including Lithuanian-rooted pastors, but characterize the institution as mixed or English-speaking rather than a canonical Lithuanian national parish. The parish remains active at 5734 10-1/2 Mile Road. Its present administrative cluster does not represent a merger, and no current Lithuanian-language ministry is documented.

historicalNarrative.text: St. Bernard began in 1920 as a Roman Catholic mission in the rural Irons area. The exact mission host, address, and pastoral dependency have not been established, so the mission phase is not assigned to the present church building.

historicalNarrative.text: The community received its first resident pastor in 1948, marking the transition from mission care to a separately staffed parish. The Diocese of Grand Rapids likewise gives 1948 as St. Bernard's establishment date, while the earlier 1920 date belongs to the mission phase rather than a competing parish founding.

sources.locator: Wolkovich, Lithuanian Religious Life in America, Vol. 3, printed p. 83, first resident pastor

historicalNarrative.text: St. Bernard's ethnic descriptions changed over time. A 1928 diocesan report called it English-speaking; a 1970 response identified Lithuanian and Bohemian composition; a later description called it mixed and originally Lithuanian. A parish leaflet attributed about three quarters of the early congregation to Lithuanian families. These descriptions support Lithuanian community history without establishing a canonical national parish.

sources.locator: Wolkovich, Lithuanian Religious Life in America, Vol. 3, printed p. 83, changing ethnic descriptions

historicalNarrative.text: Several resident pastors identified in the historical account had Lithuanian roots, among them Benjamin Marčiulionis, Albert and Ernest Bernott, and Walter Jude. Their service helps explain the parish's Lithuanian pastoral association, but shared ethnicity or clergy does not turn St. Bernard into another nearby institution or prove ethnic-parish jurisdiction.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The 1920 date belongs to St. Bernard's mission phase; 1948 marks the resident parish phase. Historical descriptions alternately call the congregation English-speaking, Lithuanian and Bohemian, mixed, or originally Lithuanian. Those variations describe membership and pastoral culture rather than competing institutions or canonical national-parish status.
